title: Some people think the servant in Matthew 25 was punished because he lost the talent.
paragraphs: Some people think the servant in Matthew 25 was punished because he lost the talent.
But that is not what happened.
He didn't lose it.
He buried it.
And that is what makes this story so unsettling.

The servant did not steal the money.
He did not waste it on reckless living.
He did not gamble it away.
When the master returned, he was even able to say something that sounded responsible:
"Look. Here is what you gave me."
He still had it.

Still intact.
Still safe.
Still untouched.
And yet the master called him wicked and lazy.
Why?
Because in the Kingdom of God, faithfulness is not measured by what you protect from risk…
It is measured by what you are willing to steward for growth.
The servant thought safety was wisdom.
But Heaven saw something different.
Heaven saw fear disguised as responsibility.
And that is the warning hidden inside this parable.
The servant himself revealed the real issue when he spoke to the master.

"I was afraid."
(Matthew 25:25)
That one sentence explains everything.
Fear made him bury what he was meant to multiply.
Fear convinced him that doing nothing was better than risking failure.
Fear made him believe that preserving the gift was enough.
But buried things do not grow.
And this is where the story becomes deeply personal for many of us.
Because not everyone destroys their calling through rebellion.
Some people lose their calling through hesitation.
Not through sin.
Through delay.
Through hiding.
Through waiting for the perfect moment that never comes.

They bury their voice.
They bury their gift.
They bury their opportunity.
They bury the assignment God placed in their hands.
Not because they hate God.
But because they are afraid.

Afraid of failing.
Afraid of criticism.
Afraid of being seen.
Afraid of stepping into responsibility.
So they convince themselves that doing nothing is safer.
But the parable exposes a powerful truth:
Unused potential is not neutral in the Kingdom of God.
When God entrusts something to a life, He expects it to move.
He expects it to grow.
He expects it to serve others.
And sometimes the greatest tragedy is not when someone ruins their gift…
It is when they hide it so deeply that it never touches the world.
Think about how many talents are buried today.
Ideas that were never started.
Ministries that were never launched.
Words that were never spoken.
Callings that were never pursued.
Acts of obedience that were delayed so long they eventually disappeared.
Not because God didn't give the talent.
But because fear convinced someone to dig a hole instead of planting a seed.
One of the most sobering parts of the story is that the servant also misunderstood his master.
He described the master as harsh.
Demanding.
Difficult.
And when your view of God becomes distorted, your stewardship becomes distorted too.
If you believe God is only waiting to punish you, you will hide.
If you believe God is impossible to please, you will hesitate.
If you believe God only wants perfection, you will never risk obedience.
But the two faithful servants understood something different.
They trusted the character of their master.
So they worked.
They invested.
They took responsibility.
They multiplied what was placed in their hands.
And when the master returned, he said something every believer longs to hear:
"Well done, good and faithful servant."
Not perfect servant.
Faithful servant.
That is the difference.
Faithfulness is not about having the biggest gift.
It is about refusing to bury what God entrusted to you.
You do not need five talents to please God.
You just need the courage to use the one you were given.
Because the real danger is not always rebellion.
Sometimes the real danger is hesitation that lasts too long.
The servant buried one talent.
But in doing so, he buried something even more tragic.
He buried his opportunity to be faithful.
And that warning still echoes today.
Some people are not running from their calling.
They are quietly hiding it in the ground.
Waiting.
Hesitating.
Delaying.
Protecting it from risk.
But buried things never multiply.
And one day, every steward will face the same question the master asked in the parable:
"What did you do with what I gave you?"
That question searches every heart.
Your gift matters.
Your calling matters.
Your obedience matters.
What God places in your hands was never meant to stay buried.
It was meant to grow.
It was meant to serve.
It was meant to multiply.
And sometimes the most dangerous prayer we can pray is not "Lord, give me more."
It is the quiet question:
"Lord… have I buried what You already gave me?"

📖 Matthew 25:25
"I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth."

Discussion Question:
What is one gift, calling, or opportunity people often bury out of fear without even realizing it?
